title: Class of 2024 Achieves Record Employment (NALP research announcement)
author: NALP (National Association for Law Placement)

dom.t: Graduate hiring: Strong outcomes mask entry contraction

st.t: Graduate hiring: Strong outcomes mask entry contraction
st.an: NALP directly supports the synthesis’s central distinction: the Class of 2024 achieved record employment despite its larger size, while reduced summer-associate hiring and a federal freeze indicated likely contraction in subsequent entry-level hiring. It also identifies smaller graduating classes as a buffer, without claiming demonstrated AI-driven displacement.
qs: However, despite graduating with approximately 3,700 more graduates than the previous class, the Class of 2024 achieved the highest ever employment rate — both overall and within bar admission required/anticipated jobs.

This figure spiked during the Great Recession, peaking at nearly 25% for the Class of 2011, and subsequently declined in each year since, except for a small pandemic-related bump in 2020 (See [Chart 2](#ch2).)  Although the market was extremely strong for the Class of 2024, future law graduates should brace for a likely contraction in BigLaw and federal hiring.

kp.k: Record employment absorbed a substantially larger graduating class
kp.d: NALP reports that the Class of 2024 achieved 93.4% employment as of March 17, 2025, approximately ten months after graduation, up 0.8 percentage points from 2023. Its entering class was about 12% larger than the Class of 2023 and other recent classes, and it produced approximately 3,700 additional graduates. These are entry-level legal employment findings; the announcement does not attribute them to AI.
qs: However, despite graduating with approximately 3,700 more graduates than the previous class, the Class of 2024 achieved the highest ever employment rate — both overall and within bar admission required/anticipated jobs.
With an overall employment rate of 93.4%, this figure was 0.8 percentage points higher than the previous record set last year by the Class of 2023.

kp.k: Attorney employment reached a classification-era high
kp.d: The proportion of graduates in bar admission required or anticipated positions rose 2.2 percentage points to 84.3%, the highest since the current job classifications began in 2001. NALP contrasts this with 64.4% for the Classes of 2012 and 2013, an increase of nearly 20 percentage points.
qs: This figure grew by 2.2 percentage points to 84.3% - marking a new all-time high dating back to when NALP introduced the current job classifications in 2001.
Overall, the percentage of jobs for which bar admission is required/anticipated has increased by nearly 20 percentage points since descending to a low of 64.4% for the Classes of 2012 and 2013.

kp.k: Overall and private-practice median salaries moved oppositely
kp.d: The overall median salary increased for a sixth consecutive year, rising 5.6% to $95,000. The private-practice median declined 3.0% to $160,000, its first decline since the Class of 2011. NALP attributes the lower private-practice median primarily to job-distribution shifts, merger-driven firm reclassification and improved salary reporting from small and mid-sized firms, rather than widespread reductions in starting salaries.
qs: For the sixth consecutive year, the overall median salary increased —climbing by 5.6% to $95,000.
However, for the first time since the Class of 2011, the median private practice salary declined, falling by 3.0% to $160,000.

Rather, the lower median salary is the result of multiple factors, including shifts in the distribution of jobs across firm sizes, the heightened merger and acquisition activity that can change how firms are categorized from year to year, and better overall salary reporting from law graduates working in small and mid-sized firms.

kp.k: Private practice hired a record number of graduates
kp.d: Private practice accounted for 58.9% of employed graduates, the highest share since 1992. The larger graduating cohort and increasing private-practice share together produced more than 2,260 additional law-firm hires relative to the Class of 2023, bringing the total to a record 20,810.
qs: Not only did the percentage of law firm jobs continue to rise this year, but with a larger class, this resulted in more than 2,260 additional graduates employed in private practice compared to the Class of 2023.
In total, 20,810 graduates obtained jobs in private practice - the highest number on record.

kp.k: Graduate law-firm jobs concentrated at firm-size extremes
kp.d: Table 2 reports that firms with 101 or more lawyers accounted for a record 47.8% of private-practice jobs in 2024, versus 25.7% in firms with 1–10 lawyers. Since the Class of 2017, the larger category has exceeded the smallest category; together these categories have accounted for at least 70% of private-practice jobs since 2000. The 101-or-more grouping is a historical survey category, not a measure of firm staffing leverage.
qs: Since the Class of 2017, the share of law firm jobs in the largest firms has once again exceeded that of the smallest firms.

Nonetheless, it remains the case that most law firm jobs are concentrated in either firms of 1-10 lawyers or firms of 101+ lawyers — with these firms accounting for at least 70% of private practice jobs since 2000.

kp.k: New graduate solo practice reached a record low
kp.d: Graduates starting their own solo practices accounted for 0.8% of law-firm jobs in 2024, a record low following a substantial decline since 2011. This category is distinct from graduates employed by existing solo practitioners, who are included in the 1–10-lawyer category.
qs: Lastly, the percentage of law firm jobs reported as solo practitioners — that is, graduates who started their own solo practice after law school — has decreased considerably since 2011 and the figure for the Class of 2024 (0.8%) was a record low.
The 1-10 category includes graduates who are working for a solo practitioner.

kp.k: Job-seeking among employed graduates fell to historic lows
kp.d: Only 6.8% of employed graduates were seeking another job. NALP interprets this as evidence of a strong market and relative employment satisfaction, rather than reporting a direct satisfaction measure. The share was typically 11–15% before the Great Recession, peaked at nearly 25% for the Class of 2011, and subsequently declined annually apart from a small pandemic-related increase in 2020.
qs: Across all employment sectors, just 6.8% of employed Class of 2024 graduates were seeking a different job, also an all-time low.
This is another indicator of the strength of the job market and demonstrates that graduates are relatively satisfied with their post-law school employment.
Prior to the Great Recession, 11-15% of graduates were typically seeking other employment.

kp.k: Large-firm and federal hiring contractions are forecast
kp.d: NALP predicts weaker BigLaw and federal hiring for subsequent graduates, distinguishing that outlook from the observed strength of 2024 outcomes. Its recruiting report documents reduced 2024 and 2025 summer associate hiring, which it takes to signal fewer large-firm graduate jobs over the next few years. It also expects the federal hiring freeze to reduce federal employment substantially for the Class of 2025; federal jobs typically represent about 3% of new graduate employment.
qs: Although the market was extremely strong for the Class of 2024, future law graduates should brace for a likely contraction in BigLaw and federal hiring.

Additionally, a federal hiring freeze enacted under the new presidential administration means that, at least for the Class of 2025, there will likely be far fewer graduates working for the federal government, a sector that typically accounts for about 3% of all new law graduate jobs.

kp.k: Smaller cohorts could cushion prospective hiring weakness
kp.d: NALP qualifies its contraction forecast by noting that the Classes of 2025 and 2026 are smaller, citing nearly 5,000 fewer entering 1Ls compared with the Class of 2024. It suggests reduced competition could preserve relatively resilient employment outcomes; this is a conditional prediction, not an observed result for those cohorts.
qs: However, the Classes of 2025 and 2026 are once again smaller classes, with nearly 5,000 fewer entering 1Ls as compared to the Class of 2024.
With fewer graduates competing for jobs, employment outcomes for these cohorts could remain relatively resilient.

kp.k: Definitions and reporting bases limit historical comparisons
kp.d: Table 1 uses graduates whose employment status was known, with specified historical exceptions; job-type classifications changed in 2001, preventing direct comparisons with earlier classifications. Its not-working category is broader than active unemployment. Table 2 excludes jobs with unreported firm size and uses only full-time law-firm jobs for 1989 and 1990, whereas other years include all law-firm jobs.
qs: New job classifications effective with the Class of 2001 preclude direct comparisons of job types with prior years.
The percentage not working includes graduates seeking employment as well as those not working or actively seeking a job.
Figures for 1989 and 1990 reflect only full-time law firm jobs; for all other years, figures reflect all law firm jobs obtained by graduates.

Percentages in this table differ slightly from those published in national reports (Employment Report & Salary Survey/Jobs & JDs) because law firm jobs for which firm size was not reported are excluded from the base.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source makes no claims or predictions about AI changing legal services.
pts.d: NALP reports graduate employment outcomes and forecasts possible contractions in large-firm and federal hiring. It does not mention AI or attribute employment trends, salary changes, or hiring forecasts to AI. These legal labour-market observations therefore do not constitute AI-impact claims.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: No evidence is offered for an AI-impact claim.
pts.d: The announcement draws on NALP employment and salary surveys, its law-student recruiting report, and a federal hiring freeze to describe employment outcomes and prospects. It provides no analysis linking those outcomes or prospects to AI; the employment figures should not be treated as findings about AI displacement or augmentation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: No AI-related timeframe or conditions are stated.
pts.d: The reported outcomes concern the Class of 2024 as of March 17, 2025. Forecasts concern large-firm hiring over the next few years and federal hiring at least for the Class of 2025, with smaller graduating cohorts potentially supporting resilience. None of these timeframes is attached to an AI-related prediction.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: No group is identified as affected by AI.
pts.d: The source discusses new law graduates, private-practice employers across firm sizes, and federal employers, but identifies no AI-driven effects on these groups.
